constraints.described_as: an unknown Arabic-looking script on the inside panel of a violin
constraints.provenance_chain: allegedly found in a violin in Boston 1968; taken to Harvard, shown to unnamed 'distinguished professors' who could not read it; Bulliet (a Columbia professor of Middle Eastern history) spent 'two decades... presenting the problem to myriad scholars' before writing a 182-page novel about it in/around 1990-91; the novel's afterword claims the inscription is real
constraints.authenticity_caveat: Schmeh's own stated view after direct investigation: 'I had serious doubts about the authenticity of this story. In spite of the myriad scholars that had allegedly occupied themselves with the message, I couldn't find a single reference to it that was not related to Bulliet's book. To me it looked like a hoax.' He then emailed Bulliet directly; Bulliet's only substantive reply was 'My novel did not find many readers, and none who had anything helpful to say about the message in the violin' and a bare assertion the violin and description are real -- no corroborating scholar, photograph provenance, or museum/collection record is named anywhere in the source
constraints.authors_own_later_hypothesis: years after the novel, Bulliet developed an unpublished hypothesis (relayed to Schmeh by email) that the script resembles handwriting on Spanish-colonial-period pamphlets he found in a Boston store, suggesting a Philippine origin during or after Spanish colonial rule -- his own hypothesis, not corroborated by any named expert
constraints.no_independent_source: Schmeh, after a dedicated search: every reference to the Sufi Fiddle inscription traces back to Bulliet's own novel and its afterword; no independent sighting, museum record, or scholarly citation was found

Cost $1, Sonnet.

2. A provenance search independent of Bulliet's own account: search OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar/Google Books for any pre-1990 (i.e. before the novel) reference to a Boston/Harvard violin inscription mystery, since Schmeh's own search (pre-2017) found none -- confirm or update that null result with the open-index tools now available (CLAUDE.md Access playbook item 3) that were not necessarily available to Schmeh's original search. Cost $1.

3. If test 1 supports the Philippine/Baybayin-family hypothesis specifically, compare the transcribed strokes against a reference Baybayin character set (a small, well-documented abugida of ~17 base characters) as a first script-identification pass -- not a decipherment, a script match. Not costed until test 1 narrows the candidate script.

cheap_test_done: 1. 25 Sept 2026, LANE B4 worker bSUF (claude-sonnet-5). Fetched Suffi-Fiddle-614.png (scienceblogs.de, 2 requests, browser UA, 2s apart; ciphers/sufi-fiddle/images/, manifest.json). The image is a hand copy of the 7 lines captioned 'copied by V. Castle Winter', overlaid on a page of English prose -- consistent with a scan from inside Bulliet's own novel, not a photograph of the violin panel. One blind single-pass sign transcription: N=165 visible signs, K=21 distinct shape-types (own sign ids, ciphers/sufi-fiddle/ciphertext.txt, two spans excluded as illegible under a crosshatched glue repair). Script checklist (sign inventory, repeats, direction, joining, diacritics) run against two reference lines stated from memory (no Wikimedia fetch made): the target matches the Arabic-script-family profile on every axis (small alphabetic inventory with high repeats, right-to-left, strong cursive joining, multi-position dot diacritics) and does NOT match Baybayin (no joining, not RTL in Baybayin). Full checklist table in ciphers/sufi-fiddle/NOTES.md. Verdict: consistent with an Arabic-derived abjad in a cursive hand (Arabic/Persian/Urdu/Ottoman/Jawi family, which includes Maranao -- the language comment #6 and the post's own 'linguist' suggested); not consistent with Baybayin specifically, despite the spec's language_candidates field using 'Philippine' as shorthand for that hypothesis. Test 3 (Baybayin character-set comparison) not triggered since test 1 did not support Baybayin specifically. No script-vs-language claim, no meaning claim, no pseudo-script verdict. Test 2 not run this pass.
